Keeping up a balance between these two stages permits the calculation to locate the best situation in a sensible measure of time. Also, these two stages permit the calculation to investigate more regions in the search space and get the global optima. In PSO algorithm, there is a single parameter named as inertia weight (ω) to achieve best optimum result. The inertia weight is used to alter the impact of the past speed on the current speed and to adjust among worldwide and nearby investigation capacities of the particle. As huge estimation of inertia weight parameter, it shows better global search capacity and the output is taken as final result in the whole solution. Similarly, when its value is little, then PSO has better local search capacity. In Standard PSO [26], no inertia weight is defined. It was first introducing by Shi and Eberhart [11] and suggested that an enormous inertia weight encourages a worldwide pursuit, while a little inertia weight encourages a neighborhood search. In traditional PSO, toward the finish of an improvement technique, the diversity of the population is small and the velocities of particles bit by bit diminished over the iteration. It shows the slow convergence rate and local optimum problem due to lack of diversity in population. Then different researcher has proposed number of inertia weight value to overcome this issue in PSO. fetched_contents.text: On the Performance of Linear Decreasing Inertia Weight Particle Swarm Optimization for Global Optimization Abstract Linear decreasing inertia weight (LDIW) strategy was introduced to improve on the performance of the original particle swarm optimization (PSO). However, linear decreasing inertia weight PSO (LDIW-PSO) algorithm is known to have the shortcoming of premature convergence in solving complex (multipeak) optimization problems due to lack of enough momentum for particles to do exploitation as the algorithm approaches its terminal point. Researchers have tried to address this shortcoming by modifying LDIW-PSO or proposing new PSO variants. Some of these variants have been claimed to outperform LDIW-PSO. The major goal of this paper is to experimentally establish the fact that LDIW-PSO is very much efficient if its parameters are properly set. First, an experiment was conducted to acquire a percentage value of the search space limits to compute the particle velocity limits in LDIW-PSO based on commonly used benchmark global optimization problems. Second, using the experimentally obtained values, five well-known benchmark optimization problems were used to show the outstanding performance of LDIW-PSO over some of its competitors which have in the past claimed superiority over it. Two other recent PSO variants with different inertia weight strategies were also compared with LDIW-PSO with the latter outperforming both in the simulation experiments conducted. 1. Introduction The idea of Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) stems from biology where a swarm of birds coordinates itself in order to achieve a goal. When a swarm of birds looks for food, its individuals will spread in the environment and move around independently with some degree of randomness which enables it to discover food accumulations. After a while, one of them will find something digestible and, being social, communicates this to its neighbors. These can then approach the source of food, thus leading to the convergence of the swarm to the source of food. Following this analogy, PSO was largely derived from sociopsychology concept and transferred to optimization [1], where each particle (bird) uses the local information regarding the displacement of its reachable closer neighbors to decide on its own displacement, resulting to complex and adaptive collective behaviors. Since the inception of PSO technique, a lot of work has been done by researchers to enhance its efficiency in handling optimization problems. One such work is the introduction of linear decreasing inertia weight (LDIW) strategy into the original PSO to control its exploration and exploitation for better performance [2–4]. However, LDIW-PSO algorithm from the literature is known to have the shortcoming of premature convergence in solving complex (multipeak) problems due to lack of enough momentum for particles to do exploitation as the algorithm approaches its terminal point. The challenge of addressing this shortcoming has been on for a long time and has attracted much attention of researchers in the field of global optimization. Consequently upon this, many other inertia weight PSO variants have been proposed [2, 5–16], with different levels of successes. Some of these variants have claimed better performances over LDIW-PSO, thereby making it look weak or inferior. Also, since improving on the performance of PSO is an area which still attracts more researchers, this paper strives to experimentally establish the fact that LDIW-PSO is very much efficient if its parameters, like velocity limits for the particles, are properly set. Using the experimentally obtained values for particle velocity limits in LDIW-PSO, results show that LDIW-PSO outperformed other PSO variants adopted for comparison. In the sections that follow, inertia weight PSO technique is described in Section 2, LDIW-PSO and the PSO variants adopted for comparison are reviewed in Section 3, parameter settings were experimentally conducted in Section 4, presentations and discussions of the experimental results of LDIW-PSO and its competing variants are made in Section 5, while Section 6 concludes the paper. 2. Particle Swarm Optimization This technique is a simple but efficient population-based, adaptive, and stochastic technique for solving simple and complex optimization problems [17, 18]. It does not need the gradient of the problems to work with, so the technique can be employed for a host of optimization problems. In PSO, a swarm of particles (set of solutions) is randomly positioned (distributed) in the search space. For every particle, the objective function determines the food at its place (value of the objective function). Every particle knows its own actual value of the objective function, its own best value (locally best solution), the best value of the whole swarm (globally best solution), and its own velocity. PSO maintains a single static population whose members are tweaked (adjust slightly) in response to new discoveries about the space. The method is essentially a form of directed mutation. It operates almost exclusively in multidimensional metric, and usually real-valued, spaces. The effect of inertia weight on particle movement and swarm dynamics is best understood as a trade-off between exploration and exploitation, with higher inertia weight favoring exploration and lower inertia weight favoring convergence and exploitation.

Higher ω increases exploration. The evidence states that a larger inertia weight “facilitates the global search” and that “a large inertia weight encourages a global pursuit,” while a smaller inertia weight encourages a local search [N2-R2][N1-F1]. Another source explicitly says that a higher inertia weight “encourages global exploration, allowing particles to move more freely and cover a larger portion of the search space” [N3-R2]. This means that when ω is high, particles retain more of their previous velocity and are less constrained by the cognitive and social components in the velocity update, so they explore the search space more broadly.

Lower ω encourages convergence and exploitation. The same sources contrast the behavior of high and low ω: a smaller inertia weight facilitates local search, and the standard PSO version without inertia weight “was first introducing by Shi and Eberhart” and “a small inertia weight encourages a neighborhood search” [N1-F1]. In practical terms, this means that when ω is low, particles are pulled more strongly toward the best solutions already found by the swarm, which speeds convergence but can reduce the ability to escape local optima. The evidence also notes that standard PSO “toward the end of an improvement technique, the diversity of the population is small and the velocities of particles bit by bit diminished over the iteration” [N1-F1], reinforcing that lower ω reduces diversity and accelerates movement toward convergence.

Inertia weight affects diversity and premature convergence. The evidence explicitly links inertia weight to premature convergence and diversity loss. The PMC study says that LDIW-PSO “is known to have the shortcoming of premature convergence in solving complex (multipeak) optimization problems due to lack of enough momentum for particles to do exploitation as the algorithm approaches its terminal point” [N5-F2]. The same source also states that LDIW-PSO’s performance depends on parameter settings and that its velocity limits were experimentally determined to improve performance [N5-F2]. This implies that a fixed or overly decreasing inertia weight can prematurely reduce diversity and cause convergence to local optima. Conversely, higher ω preserves diversity and supports broader exploration, while too low ω can cause premature convergence by making particles move too closely together and lose global search ability.

Taken together, inertia weight shapes particle movement by controlling how much of the previous velocity is carried forward, how much new movement is generated by the cognitive and social components, and thus how the swarm balances exploration against convergence. The evidence consistently supports the interpretation that ω is a critical design knob for controlling these dynamics [N2-R1][N2-R2][N3-R2][N5-F2].

The overview cites constant inertia weight, random inertia weight, chaotic inertia weight, and linearly decreasing inertia weight, among others [N1-F1]. It also mentions a time-varying inertia weight (TVIW) scheme that decreases over time, allowing “more global search ability at the beginning of the run and more local search ability near the end of the run” [N1-F1]. How ω is tuned depends on the problem type and dimensions. This implies that for high-dimensional or complex problems, a larger ω may be needed to maintain diversity and exploration, while for simpler or more constrained problems, a lower ω may accelerate convergence. The evidence also notes that PSO is sensitive to parameter tuning overall, including inertia weight, and that these parameters need tuning to work well on any problem [N1-F1].

ω interacts with other PSO parameters like acceleration coefficients. The theoretical explanation of the velocity update equation with inertia weight centers on the standard form of the PSO velocity update and the role of ω in preserving or reducing previous velocity.

The standard velocity update formula is commonly written as a weighted combination of the previous velocity, the cognitive component, and the social component. The overview provides the standard velocity update as:

$$
v_{i,j}^{n+1} = w \cdot v_{i,j}^n + c_1 \cdot r_1 \cdot (p_{i,j}^n - x_{i,j}^n) + c_2 \cdot r_2 \cdot (p_g,j^n - x_{i,j}^n)
$$

where $w$ is the inertia weight, $c_1$ and $c_2$ are acceleration coefficients, $r_1$ and $r_2$ are random numbers, $p_{i,j}^n$ is the particle’s personal best, and $p_g,j^n$ is the global best [N1-F1]. A simpler version from the search material also states that the velocity is updated in the form $v_i(k+1) = w v_i(k) + \rho_1 c_1(\dots)$, and that the position update is influenced by the particle’s velocity [N6-R3]. This is consistent with the standard PSO formulation and shows that ω appears as the coefficient multiplying the previous velocity term.

How ω controls the persistence of previous velocity is straightforward: a larger ω means the previous velocity has a stronger influence on the new velocity, while a smaller ω means the previous velocity is discounted more strongly [N1-F1]. The overview explicitly states that the inertia weight “is used to alter the impact of the past speed on the current speed” [N1-F1]. This means that ω acts as a momentum term, preserving velocity history to some extent and reducing abrupt changes in direction.

How the inertia term interacts with cognitive and social components is central to PSO’s behavior. In the standard equation, the cognitive component is $c_1 \cdot r_1 \cdot (p_i - x_i)$, which pulls the particle toward its personal best, and the social component is $c_2 \cdot r_2 \cdot (p_g - x_i)$, which pulls the particle toward the global best [N1-F1][N6-R3]. The inertia term $w \cdot v_i^n$ interacts with these components by determining how much the particle’s previous movement is retained versus how much the cognitive and social forces dominate the new velocity. When ω is large, the previous velocity dominates and the cognitive/social terms have less influence; when ω is small, the cognitive and social terms can more strongly guide the next velocity [N1-F1][N1-R3]. The overview also notes that the inertia weight “is used to balance the global exploration and local exploitation,” and that a large inertia weight encourages a global pursuit while a small inertia weight encourages a neighborhood search [N1-F1][N2-R2]. This shows that ω is not merely a velocity preservation factor but a structural parameter that controls the trade-off between exploration and exploitation in the algorithm.

Taken together, the evidence supports a clear theoretical interpretation: the standard velocity update equation with inertia weight is a weighted combination of previous velocity, cognitive movement, and social movement, where ω determines how much the previous velocity is carried forward and thus how strongly the particle’s motion is influenced by memory versus by the current best solutions [N1-F1][N6-R3][N2-R2].

## Integrated final explanation of inertia weight in Particle Swarm Optimization

Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) is a population-based search algorithm in which particles move through a search space to find optimal solutions. A central design parameter in PSO is the **inertia weight ω**, which controls the balance between **exploration** (global search) and **exploitation** (local search). Incorporating ω into the velocity update equation changes the way particles move and how the swarm evolves over time. The evidence across the branch reports is consistent: ω is not a simple “friction” term; it is a structural knob that determines how much a particle’s previous motion is preserved, how strongly the cognitive and social components influence the next step, and how the swarm explores versus converges [N1-F1][N2-R2][N6-R3].

---

## 1) Theoretical effect on the velocity update equation

The standard PSO velocity update equation is a weighted combination of the particle’s previous velocity, the cognitive component, and the social component. The branch report gives a canonical form:

$$
v_{i,j}^{n+1} = w \cdot v_{i,j}^n + c_1 \cdot r_1 \cdot (p_{i,j}^n - x_{i,j}^n) + c_2 \cdot r_2 \cdot (p_g,j^n - x_{i,j}^n)
$$

where $w$ is the inertia weight, $c_1$ and $c_2$ are acceleration coefficients, $r_1$ and $r_2$ are random numbers, $p_{i,j}^n$ is the particle’s personal best, and $p_g,j^n$ is the global best [N1-F1]. A simpler version from the evidence also states that the velocity is updated as $v_i(k+1) = w v_i(k) + \rho_1 c_1(\dots)$, and that the position update is influenced by the particle’s velocity [N6-R3]. This confirms that ω appears explicitly as the coefficient multiplying the previous velocity term.

### How ω controls the persistence of previous velocity

The key role of ω is to determine how much of the previous velocity is carried forward into the new velocity. A larger ω means the previous velocity has a stronger influence, while a smaller ω means the previous velocity is discounted more strongly [N1-F1]. The branch report states that inertia weight “is used to alter the impact of the past speed on the current speed” [N1-F1]. This means ω acts as a **momentum term**—it preserves velocity history to some extent and reduces abrupt changes in direction.

### How the inertia term interacts with cognitive and social components

The inertia term interacts directly with the cognitive and social components of the velocity update. The cognitive component pulls the particle toward its own best position, while the social component pulls it toward the global best [N1-F1][N6-R3]. When ω is large, the previous velocity dominates, and the cognitive/social components have relatively less influence; when ω is small, the cognitive and social terms can more strongly guide the next velocity [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that the inertia weight is used to **balance global exploration and local exploitation** [N1-F1][N2-R2]. This is central: ω is not just a velocity preservation factor; it is a structural parameter that determines the algorithm’s search behavior.

---

## 2) Effect on particle movement and swarm dynamics

The effect of inertia weight on particle movement is best understood as a trade-off between exploration and exploitation. The branch report states that **higher ω increases exploration**, while **lower ω encourages convergence and exploitation** [N2-R2][N3-R2]. This is because a larger inertia weight facilitates global search and encourages a global pursuit, whereas a smaller inertia weight facilitates local search and encourages a neighborhood search [N1-F1]. Another source explicitly says that a higher inertia weight “encourages global exploration, allowing particles to move more freely and cover a larger portion of the search space” [N3-R2]. In contrast, a smaller inertia weight reduces diversity and accelerates movement toward convergence, as the standard PSO version without inertia weight “toward the end of an improvement technique, the diversity of the population is small and the velocities of particles bit by bit diminished over the iteration” [N1-F1].

### How inertia weight affects diversity and premature convergence

The evidence also shows that inertia weight directly affects diversity and premature convergence. The branch report notes that LDIW-PSO is known to suffer from premature convergence in complex multipeak problems due to a lack of enough momentum for particles to do exploitation as the algorithm approaches its terminal point [N5-F2]. This implies that a fixed or overly decreasing inertia weight can prematurely reduce diversity and cause convergence to local optima. In contrast, higher ω preserves diversity and supports broader exploration, while too low ω can cause premature convergence by making particles move too closely together and lose global search ability [N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-F2].

In short, inertia weight shapes particle movement by controlling:
- how much the previous velocity is retained,
- how much the cognitive and social components influence the new velocity, and
- the overall balance between exploration and convergence [N1-F1][N2-R2][N3-R2].

---

## 3) Practical implications and design choices for choosing ω

Choosing ω is a practical design decision that depends on the inertia weight schemes available and the problem being solved. The branch report shows that inertia weight is not a single fixed constant in standard PSO; instead, it is often time-varying or adaptive [N1-F1]. Common schemes include constant, linearly decreasing, and nonlinear or dynamic variants. The evidence cites constant inertia weight, random inertia weight, chaotic inertia weight, linearly decreasing inertia weight, and others [N1-F1]. It also mentions time-varying inertia weight (TVIW), which decreases over time to allow “more global search ability at the beginning of the run and more local search ability near the end of the run” [N1-F1].

### Trade-offs among common schemes

Each scheme has different trade-offs:
- Constant ω is simple but may not adapt well to changing search dynamics [N1-F1].
- Linearly decreasing ω can reduce premature convergence but may lose too much momentum near the end [N5-F2].
- Dynamic schemes attempt to maintain a better balance through time-varying or nonlinear adjustment [N1-F1].

### Tuning ω for different problem types and dimensions

The evidence says that larger inertia weights are suitable for large-scale exploration, while smaller inertia weights are suitable for small-scale mining [N1-R3]. The benchmark study on LDIW-PSO emphasizes that the algorithm’s performance depends on parameter settings, including velocity limits, and that it can outperform competitors when properly tuned [N5-F2]. This means that for high-dimensional or complex problems, a larger ω may be needed to maintain diversity and exploration, while for simpler or more constrained problems, a lower ω may accelerate convergence. The branch report also notes that PSO is sensitive to parameter tuning and that these parameters need tuning to work well on any problem [N1-F1].

### Interaction with other PSO parameters

The evidence explicitly states that ω interacts with acceleration coefficients $c_1$ and $c_2$, which define the magnitude of the influences on velocity in the directions of the local and global optima [N1-F1]. It also discusses time-varying acceleration coefficients (TVAC), in which $c_1$ decreases and $c_2$ increases over time [N1-F1]. This means that ω should not be set in isolation but must be coordinated with $c_1$, $c_2$, and other parameters to achieve the desired balance [N1-F1].

---

## 4) Empirical evidence and benchmark comparisons across inertia weight strategies

Empirical evidence shows that no single inertia weight strategy dominates all problems. The branch report states that performance varies strongly with problem complexity, dimensionality, and the choice of inertia weight strategy [N5-F2][N1-F1]. LDIW-PSO is cited as an example where a well-tuned linearly decreasing inertia weight can outperform competitors when its parameters are properly set [N5-F2]. The same study also compares LDIW-PSO with two other recent PSO variants with different inertia weight strategies and finds that LDIW-PSO outperforms both in simulation experiments [N5-F2]. This suggests that a well-tuned linearly decreasing strategy can be competitive, but the best variant depends on the benchmark set and problem instance.

### Which variants perform best?

The evidence indicates that more sophisticated dynamic strategies can improve the balance between global and local search [N1-F1]. It also notes that nonlinear inertia weight updating is described as a way to improve the balance between global and local search [N1-F1]. This implies that benchmark results often favor strategies that adapt the inertia weight over time rather than fix it at a constant value.

### How performance varies with problem complexity and dimensionality

The evidence shows that performance varies with problem complexity and dimensionality. LDIW-PSO is known to suffer from premature convergence on complex (multipeak) optimization problems due to lack of enough momentum for exploitation near the terminal point [N5-F2]. This implies that more complex problems benefit from inertia weight schemes that maintain sufficient exploration and momentum, while simpler problems may tolerate lower ω and faster convergence. The evidence also emphasizes that PSO is sensitive to parameter tuning and that these parameters need tuning to work well on any problem [N1-F1], which means higher-dimensional problems may require more careful adjustment of ω and related parameters to avoid premature convergence or insufficient exploration.

### Study limitations and caveats

The empirical evidence also highlights important limitations. The benchmark study on LDIW-PSO notes that its performance depends on parameter settings, especially velocity limits, and that its earlier reputation as weak or inferior was challenged by experimental results [N5-F2]. This suggests that benchmark comparisons are sensitive to implementation details and tuning choices. The evidence also notes that many inertia weight variants have been proposed with different levels of success, and that improving PSO remains an active research area [N5-F2]. This implies that benchmark results should be interpreted carefully and not overgeneralized.

---

## 5) Integrated conclusion

Incorporating the inertia weight ω into PSO changes the velocity update equation in a fundamental way: it makes the new velocity a weighted combination of the previous velocity, the cognitive component, and the social component. A larger ω preserves more of the previous velocity and favors global exploration, while a smaller ω discounts the previous velocity and encourages convergence and exploitation [N1-F1][N2-R2][N3-R2]. The inertia term interacts directly with the cognitive and social components, determining how much the particle’s motion is guided by memory versus by the current best solutions [N1-F1][N6-R3].

In terms of particle movement and swarm dynamics, higher ω increases exploration and diversity, while lower ω increases convergence and exploitation. However, too low a ω can lead to premature convergence, and too high a ω can slow convergence and reduce exploitation [N2-R2][N3-R2][N5-F2]. Practically, ω is not a fixed parameter but is often chosen from a range of schemes, including constant, linearly decreasing, and dynamic variants, with trade-offs between exploration, exploitation, and convergence speed [N1-F1][N5-F2]. Tuning ω depends on the problem type, dimensionality, and other PSO parameters, and the best choice often requires careful experimentation [N1-F1][N5-F2].

Overall, inertia weight is a central design knob in PSO that controls the algorithm’s ability to explore the search space, converge to good solutions, and avoid premature convergence. The evidence supports a nuanced view: there is no universally best ω, and the best strategy depends on the problem and the choice of inertia weight scheme [N1-F1][N5-F2].
